A Smaller World

Oil, Terror, and the Screen

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

Over the last fifty years the world has grown smaller. Oil carried across the sea tied the wealth of rich nations to the politics of the Middle East. New weapons and new networks allowed a small group to strike at a great power. And new ways of sending words and pictures have made every event seem close at hand. This lesson follows these three threads: dependence, grievance, and speed. As you read, ask what each did for free peoples, and what each cost them. This is the question of this module, and of the Quarter 4 Capstone.

Objectives
  1. Explain why oil gave the Middle East such weight in world affairs after 1973.
  2. Describe the rise of al-Qaeda, the attacks of September 11, 2001, and the American response.
  3. Explain how the internet and satellite news changed the speed at which events and ideas spread.
Quick Check-in

The world's oil lies far from the nations that burn it. What do you think a nation that depends on imports risks most?

Why Oil Mattered
Historical Figure
Osama bin Ladenoh-SAH-mah bin LAH-den

Osama bin Laden (1957 to 2011) was born in Saudi Arabia to a family that had grown rich in the building trade. He went to Afghanistan in the 1980s to help the Afghan rebels against the Soviet Union, and there he built a network of fighters. After the Gulf War he turned against Saudi Arabia and the United States.

In 1996 and again in 1998 he issued statements that called on his followers to kill Americans. Al-Qaeda carried out a series of attacks that grew larger, until September 11, 2001. For ten years he hid, and in May 2011 American commandos found him in a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, and killed him.

Historical Figure
George W. BushJORJ DUB-ul-yoo BOOSH

George W. Bush (born 1946) is the son of the forty-first president, George H. W. Bush. He studied at Yale and Harvard, worked in the oil business, and was elected governor of Texas in 1994. He won the presidency in 2000 in a contest decided by the Supreme Court after a close vote in Florida.

The attacks of September 11 came in his first year in office. He declared a war on terror, sent troops to Afghanistan and Iraq, and set up the Department of Homeland Security. His decision to invade Iraq is still argued over. He left office in 2009, in the midst of a deep financial crisis.

Where Could It Have Gone Differently?

Technology
The World Wide Web

The internet is a network that links computers around the world. It began in the late 1960s as a project of the American defense department, and universities soon joined. It was hard to use. In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee, working at the laboratory called CERN, proposed a system of pages joined by links, each with its own address. The first website went online in 1991.

Berners-Lee did not charge for the idea, and in 1993 CERN made the software free for all. Browsers that showed pictures followed, and the web spread quickly. It changed how people learn, shop, work, and argue. It also made it easy to spread false information, and hard to tell what is true.

Oil, Terror, and the Screen

Part 1

Oil and Dependence

Chapter 1The Embargo
Chapter 2Iran and the Gulf War
Chapter 1

The Embargo

Modern economies run on oil, and much of the world’s oil lies under the Middle East. American oil production peaked in 1970, and after that the United States relied more on imports. In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, the Arab members of an oil group called OAPEC placed an embargo on oil sales to the United States and other supporters of Israel. Prices rose to four times what they had been. Americans waited in long lines at gas stations, and the economies of the West stalled. The embargo ended in 1974, but it had taught a lesson about dependence.

Chapter 2

Iran and the Gulf War

In 1979 a revolution in Iran drove out the shah, a close ally of the United States. The new ruler was the ayatollah Khomeini, who called America the great enemy. In November 1979 students seized the American embassy in Tehran and held fifty-two Americans for 444 days. Oil prices doubled again. In August 1990 Iraq’s dictator, Saddam Hussein, invaded Kuwait and threatened Saudi Arabia, the greatest oil producer. A coalition of thirty-four nations, led by the United States and approved by the United Nations, drove his army from Kuwait in six weeks in early 1991. American troops stayed in Saudi Arabia, the land of Islam’s holiest places. The United Nations kept sanctions on Iraq for years.

Part 2

Grievance and Terror

Chapter 3Bin Laden and al-Qaeda
Chapter 4September 11 and After
Chapter 3

Bin Laden and al-Qaeda

The presence of those troops angered a Saudi millionaire, Osama bin Laden, who had fought the Soviets in Afghanistan. He founded a network called al-Qaeda, and in 1996 he declared war on the United States. He wanted the Americans out of Muslim lands and the Saudi royal family overthrown. terrorism was his chosen tool. In 1993 a bomb damaged the World Trade Center in New York. In 1998 truck bombs at the American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania killed more than two hundred. In 2000 a boat full of explosives struck the destroyer Cole in Yemen. All of these were warnings. Al-Qaeda found a home in Afghanistan, where the Taliban, a harsh movement of religious students, had taken power in 1996.

Chapter 4

September 11 and After

On the morning of September 11, 2001, nineteen men seized four airliners. Two were flown into the towers of the World Trade Center, which collapsed, and one into the Pentagon. The passengers on the fourth plane fought the hijackers, and it crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. In all, 2,977 people were killed. Millions watched the second tower being struck live on television. NATO, for the first time in its history, said that the attack on one member was an attack on all. In your reading in this module, President George W. Bush speaks to Congress and to the nation about what happened.

In October 2001 American and allied forces entered Afghanistan, and the Taliban fell within weeks. Bin Laden escaped, and he was killed by American commandos in Pakistan in 2011. In 2003 the United States and a few allies invaded Iraq and overthrew Saddam Hussein, on the ground, among others, that he held weapons of mass destruction. None were found, and the war became long and divided Americans and their allies. In 2021, after twenty years, the last American troops left Afghanistan and the Taliban returned to power. Americans still argue over the costs, and over what freedom required.

Part 3

The Screen and the Speed

Chapter 5The Screen
Chapter 6A Smaller World
Chapter 5

The Screen

A third thread is speed. In 1980 an American company began the first television news channel to run twenty-four hours a day. In 1991 the Gulf War was shown live. In 1989 a British scientist at a laboratory in Switzerland, Tim Berners-Lee, proposed what he called the World Wide Web, which turned a network used by scientists into a tool for everyone. By the early 2000s hundreds of millions of people were online. Facebook began in 2004, YouTube in 2005, Twitter in 2006, and in 2007 the iPhone put the internet into a pocket. social media allowed anyone to send words and pictures to thousands at once, without an editor.

The effect was large, and it cut both ways. In December 2010 a Tunisian street vendor set himself on fire in protest against the police. Phone videos of the protests spread across the Arab world, and within weeks the rulers of Tunisia and Egypt had fallen. Many hoped for free government. But in most of these countries the old rulers returned or war followed, and in Syria a civil war killed hundreds of thousands and drove millions into exile. The same tools helped terrorists to spread their message and recruit followers. Rumors now moved faster than facts could be checked. News of a bank failure in New York in September 2008 sent a financial panic around the world within days. A new virus that appeared in one Chinese city in late 2019 had reached every continent within months.

Chapter 6

A Smaller World

This is part of what is called globalization. Trade, travel, and money flow across borders more freely than ever. China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, and its factories became the workshop of the world. Goods became cheaper, and many millions escaped poverty. But the same ties made nations depend on one another, and on distant makers of goods, in ways that a sudden shock could break.

You have now seen the way free peoples met claims of right against the state, in South Africa, the American South, and the Balkans, and the pressures of oil, terror, and speed. Does a smaller world make free peoples safer or more exposed? Make two lists. One holds the evidence for safer: shared markets, alliances such as NATO, quick aid for the afflicted, and the pressure of world opinion. The other holds the evidence for more exposed: dependence on oil and distant factories, terror networks, and the speed of rumor and panic. Mark where the two lists overlap, since many things on one belong on the other. Keep all of your notes from this quarter. You will use them for the Quarter 4 Capstone.
